# The provenance file on Wiraqucha

*The provenance file for Wiraqucha. Nothing here is unsourced; that is what the file is for.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **—**, from the tradition's own record. On record: Juan de Betanzos, Suma y Narración de los Incas (1551), chapters 1–2 (the flood, the creation of nations, the weeping journey), Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Book 13, chapter 3 (creation and Titicaca), Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica, chapters 6–7 (the 1572 inquiry of Cusco), Martín de Murúa, Historia general del Piru (1616), on the Coricancha image and the name.

**2. The narrative record.** **The Flood of Unu Pachakuti** — Juan de Betanzos, whose Suma y Narración de los Incas (1551) is the fullest early account, tells that Wiraqucha made the first people at Tiwanaku and gave them the world to keep; but they grew proud and lived without worship, so he resolved to undo them.  He sent a great flood — unu pachakuti, a watery overturning of the world — that drowned the first race, the wari, while he himself rose into the sky above Titicaca. **The Making of Nations at Tiwanaku** — Father Bernabé Cobo's Historia del Nuevo Mundo (Book 13) preserves the imperial version: after the flood, Wiraqucha set to work at Tiwanaku, where he sculpted the forms of all the nations to come — each with its own face, dress, language, songs, and seeds — and brought them to life.  When the work was done he dispatched them, calling them out of caves, springs, and rivers to find their homelands: one nation he sent by way of a cave, another along a river's course, and to the Inca ancestors he gave the special charge that would lead them at last to Cusco.

**3. The physical record.** Wiraqucha's archaeology is the archaeology of his stage. Tiwanaku, the great center of the altiplano (c. 500–1000 CE), holds the Kalasasaya platform, the monumental Gateway of the Sun, and the precision-cut blocks of Puma Punku — the ruins later tradition named as his workshop, where the myth says he modeled the nations in stone. On the Island of the Sun and Island of the Moon in Lake Titicaca, Inca pilgrims' shrines — the Chincana labyrinths, the sacred rock, the sanctuary terraces — mark the myth's exact geography, and Copacabana's basilica stands on the shore where the ritual boats once left. In Cusco, the chroniclers describe a solid-gold image of the god in the Coricancha (Cobo; Murúa), melted down within years of 1532. No pre-Columbian inscription names him: the ruins give the stage, and the chronicles give the script.

**4. The current holding.** The temple at [/viracocha/](/viracocha/), classified Tier 2. One decisive feature survives — a single, honest mark — which places the restoration in Tier-2: exact, and exactly labeled.

**5. The documented resonances.** **Solar & Renewable Energy**, **Aviation & Aerospace**, **Space, Astronomy & Celestial Science** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/viracocha/blog/resonance/).

**6. The continuing record.** Wiraqucha never lost his mountain.  Pilgrims still cross to the Island of the Sun and Moon on Titicaca, and each June solstice thousands gather at Tiwanaku to watch the sun rise through the Gate of the Sun — a rite older than any written version of the myth it now frames.
